MultipleChoice.prompt: A session has a fixed question cap shared among carried-over questions, due reviews and new concepts from the change. After carried questions are counted, some slots remain open. Why does the split_slots approach (reserve half the open slots, rounded up, for new concepts; give due reviews the remainder; let new concepts use any unused slots) behave better than simply filling due reviews first?
options: Carried questions and reviews share the cap, and new concepts are only asked when both of those leave room.
The cap is divided into fixed halves for the whole session, so unused review slots are simply dropped when there are few due reviews.
The cap is applied separately to reviews and to new concepts, so a session can ask up to the cap of each.
Half the open slots, rounded up, are reserved for new concepts and reviews get the rest, so a large review backlog cannot starve the change, while unused reviews slots can go to new concepts.
Reviews are filled first and new concepts get whatever is left, because reviews are overdue and must not be postponed.
reasons: This makes new concepts the lowest priority, which would let reviews starve the change. The function reserves a share for new concepts precisely to prevent that.
The split applies only to open slots and is not rigid: new concepts can take any unused slots. Dropping them would waste question budget and shortchange the change.
The cap is a single ceiling shared among carried questions, reviews and new concepts. Applying it per category would exceed the budget.

Reserving a guaranteed share for new concepts means a big backlog of reviews cannot crowd out questions about the change, and letting new concepts absorb unused slots keeps the budget fully used. Reviews still get the remainder, so a change with little new material still gets its reviews.
This is the opposite of the design. Filling reviews first lets a backlog of due reviews consume the whole budget and crowd out questions about the change itself.

questions.explanation: Reserving a guaranteed share for new concepts means a big backlog of reviews cannot crowd out questions about the change, and letting new concepts absorb unused slots keeps the budget fully used. Reviews still get the remainder, so a change with little new material still gets its reviews.

Open.prompt: A tool extracts concepts from a code change and tags each with a weight (Core, Supporting, or Incidental). When composing quiz questions, it skips Incidental concepts and concepts the author already knows (their review card is not yet due), and it orders Core concepts before Supporting ones. As a result, some changes now produce zero questions. Explain why this filtering and ordering is useful, and why allowing zero questions to be a valid outcome is a sound design choice rather than a bug. Also describe one risk of this approach and how a lenient parse of the model's weight output affects it.
Open.rubric:
A good answer must cover:
- Purpose of weighting/ordering: limits questions to concepts central to the change, so the quiz stays short and focused and Core concepts are asked first, especially if there is a cap on question count.
- Purpose of skipping known concepts: a review card that isn't due means the author has recently shown understanding (spaced repetition), so re-asking is redundant, wastes effort, and causes quiz fatigue.
- Why zero questions is valid: if everything is Incidental or already known, there is nothing worth checking; forcing a question would produce low-value or trivia questions and reduce trust in the tool, and could block the author needlessly.
- A risk: mis-weighting (a truly important concept labeled Incidental, or a hallucinated weight) or a stale or over-trusted 'known' status could let the author skip real gaps in understanding; zero questions could be mistaken for a pass of verification.
- Lenient parsing: handling variant or malformed weight strings from the model (e.g. casing, unknown values falling back to a default) prevents a whole extraction from failing, but the choice of default matters (a default of Supporting/Core is safer than Incidental, which would silently drop concepts).

Common misconceptions that make an answer wrong:
- Claiming zero questions means the tool is broken or that at least one question must always be asked.
- Saying known-concept skipping means the concept was never extracted or that the author has permanently mastered it.
- Describing weight as only a display label with no effect on which questions are asked or in what order.
- Ignoring that a due review card means the concept is still eligible to be asked.

questions.explanation: A good answer says that weighting and filtering keep questions focused on what matters and avoid re-quizzing concepts the author has already demonstrated they know. It also covers that zero questions is a legitimate result when nothing important or new remains, and that forcing a minimum would add noise and erode trust in the tool.

MultipleChoice.prompt: A PR gets a new CI round after the previous round was superseded by a new push before the author answered some of its questions, and the question cap has since been lowered. What does the new round do with those unanswered questions?
options: It re-asks the latest round's unanswered questions unchanged first, counts them against the cap, and adds new questions about the diff since the latest round that asked its own questions, even if the cap is already reached by the carried ones.
It treats the superseded ungraded round's concepts as already covered and skips them, asking new questions only about concepts not yet seen on the PR.
It re-asks every question from all earlier rounds, answered or not, then adds questions about the whole PR diff from the base branch.
It re-asks the earlier unanswered questions only if there is room under the current cap, and otherwise silently drops the overflow so the cap is never exceeded.
It drops the earlier unanswered questions, because the new round's diff supersedes them, and asks only fresh questions about the new commits up to the cap.
reasons: Carried questions come first, are unchanged, and count against the cap but are never dropped. Because the round was superseded without being graded, its concepts are not skipped, so the author still has to show understanding of them.
Concepts from ungraded, superseded rounds are explicitly not skipped. Skipping them would mean a concept could never be examined if its round was superseded before it was graded.

Only the latest round's unanswered questions are carried, not answered ones or those from all rounds. New questions target the diff since the latest round that asked its own questions, not the whole PR.
The carried questions are never dropped, even if the cap was lowered since. The cap limits how many new questions are added after the carried ones, not whether carried ones survive.
This reverses the behavior: superseded rounds do not discard their unanswered questions. Dropping them would let an author avoid a question simply by pushing another commit.

questions.explanation: Carried questions come first, are unchanged, and count against the cap but are never dropped. Because the round was superseded without being graded, its concepts are not skipped, so the author still has to show understanding of them.
